question.text: Does elective re-siting of intravenous cannulae decrease peripheral thrombophlebitis?
question.context: Peripheral venous thrombophlebitis (PVT) is a common complication of intravenous cannulation, occurring in about 30% of patients. We evaluated the effect of elective re-siting of intravenous cannulae every 48 hours on the incidence and severity of PVT in patients receiving intravenous fluids/drugs. We randomized 42 patients who were admitted for major abdominal surgery to either the control or study group (n = 21 in either group). Informed consent was obtained from all of them. Cannulae in the control group were removed only if the site became painful, the cannula got dislodged or there were signs and symptoms suggestive of PVT, namely pain, erythema, swelling, excessive warmth or a palpable venous cord. Cannulae in the study group were changed and re-sited electively every 48 hours. All the patients were examined every 24 hours for signs and symptoms of PVT at the current and previous sites of infusion. The incidence of PVT was 100% (21/21) in the control group and only 9.5% (2/21) in the study group (p<0.0001). The severity of PVT was also less in the study group compared with that in the control group. Day-wise correlation of the incidence of PVT showed that 82.6% of the episodes of PVT occurred on day 3.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study clearly demonstrates a significant reduction in the incidence of peripheral thrombophlebitis in the group where cannulae were re-sited electively every 48 hours compared to the control group where cannulae were removed only when symptomatic. This strongly suggests that elective re-siting decreases the risk of PVT.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The incidence of PVT was 100% (21/21) in the control group and only 9.5% (2/21) in the study group (p<0.0001).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could contribute to PVT, the study design and the magnitude of the difference in incidence make elective re-siting the most likely cause of the observed reduction.

The data shows a clear benefit with both incidence and severity of PVT reduced in the re-siting group.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The statistically significant reduction in PVT incidence (100% vs 9.5%) with p<0.0001 demonstrates the effectiveness of elective re-siting
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No other interventions were mentioned in the study that could explain the reduction in PVT, making elective re-siting the most likely effective measure

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other possible interventions (e.g., using different cannula sites, anticoagulation) were not compared here, but the clear difference in PVT incidence between the groups due to the re-siting protocol makes it the best-supported answer.
